steps.title: Same ordinals, different gender
body: Telling time used feminine ordinals because السَّاعَة is feminine. Dates use the exact same roots — ثَانِي، ثَالِث، رَابِع، خَامِس… — but in their masculine form, because يَوْم (day) is masculine. أَوَّل (1st) breaks the pattern on purpose: it's its own irregular word, not built the way the others are.

A date is just [ordinal] + مِنْ + [month]: الثَّالِثُ مِنْ سِبْتَمْبِر (the third of September) — a complete phrase, no verb needed, the same shape telling time already used. Add هُوَ to make it a full sentence: الْيَوْمَ هُوَ الْخَامِسُ مِنْ مَارِس (today is the fifth of March).
The twelve month names here are the ones used across most of the Arab world — Egypt, the Gulf, the Maghreb. Some countries (the Levant, Iraq) use an older, different set of names instead.

steps.title: First to tenth, January to December

steps.title: Masculine, not feminine
steps.prompt: Why الثَّالِثُ (masculine) here, not الثَّالِثَة (the feminine form used for telling time)?
steps.explanation: The ordinal agrees with whatever noun it's really describing — السَّاعَة (feminine) for time, يَوْم (masculine) for dates. Same roots, different gender.

steps.title: The one irregular one
steps.prompt: Does أَوَّل follow the same pattern as ثَانِي، ثَالِث، رَابِع…؟

options.label: No — it's irregular, its own separate word
Yes, exactly the same فَاعِل pattern

steps.explanation: أَوَّل doesn't come from the same root-pattern as the others — it's simply memorized on its own, the way a1 و12 were for cardinal numbers.

steps.title: What does هُوَ point to?
steps.prompt: What does هُوَ refer back to?
steps.explanation: هُوَ agrees with يَوْم (day), the masculine noun اليوم implicitly stands for — the same way a pronoun always refers back to something already established.

steps.title: You've finished Numbers, Counting & Time
steps.message: Counting, the clock, prices, and now dates — all four pieces of this unit are done. You've seen Arabic's numbers work in three different ways (1-2, 3-10, 11-99) and its ordinals in two genders, all built from the same small set of roots.
